programs.label: Public housing

entries.text: Eligibility screening, assigned priorities and required apartment size govern offers. Applicants who live, work or will work in NYC receive a preference over those who do not.
Income and household composition are reexamined annually. NYCHA verifies the household information and recalculates rent under its continued-occupancy rules.
An authorized household member may succeed to a lease after the tenant leaves or dies. Permanent permission, continuous residence and remaining-family-member eligibility govern that decision.
Transfers use priorities, certification date and required apartment size. NYCHA’s transfer priorities distinguish one excess bedroom from two or more against its occupancy standard.

programs.label: Rent-stabilized

entries.authority: Owner · vacancy lease under rent regulation
entries.text: A new tenancy begins with a vacancy lease for a regulated apartment. The lease and rent remain subject to rent-stabilization rules.

entries.authority: Owner · statutory renewal obligation; HCR · oversight
entries.text: Tenants generally have the right to choose a one- or two-year renewal on the same terms and conditions, with lawful rent adjustments. HCR receives complaints when an owner fails to offer renewal.

Qualifying family members who shared the apartment as their primary residence may inherit renewal rights. The general co-residence period is two years, reduced to one for seniors or disabled people; inception-of-tenancy, relationship and temporary-absence provisions also apply.

programs.label: Rent-controlled

entries.text: NYC rent control generally covers qualifying pre-1947 buildings with continuous occupancy dating from before July 1971. Qualifying family succession can continue the tenancy.
Renewal leases are not required. Rent increases are limited under the Maximum Base Rent system, and services and eviction are regulated.
Qualifying family members may retain rent-control protection when the tenant dies or permanently leaves. HCR’s family and primary-residence criteria govern succession.

programs.scope: NYCHA tenant-based Housing Choice Vouchers. HPD and HCR operate separate NYC programs.

entries.text: The agency determines voucher eligibility. A voucher holder searches for a privately owned home; the unit must meet program requirements before assistance begins.

entries.authority: Housing agency · subsidy administration; owner · lease
entries.text: Assistance is paid to the owner on the participant’s behalf. Continuing participation includes household recertification and unit inspections.

After the voucher holder dies or leaves, NYCHA determines whether a remaining permanent household member can continue receiving assistance under its occupancy and succession policy. Household status, continued eligibility and legal-capacity or guardian requirements apply; voucher succession is separate from tenancy succession.

entries.authority: Administering agency · transfer and portability rules
entries.text: Moving assistance is governed by the administering agency’s current transfer and portability rules. The voucher program and the apartment’s underlying rent regulation are separate layers.

programs.label: Rent Freeze · combined SCRIE / DRIE
programs.scope: SCRIE and DRIE, layered onto eligible existing housing.

entries.authority: DOF · SCRIE / DRIE; HPD · specified SCRIE housing
entries.text: Age or disability, income, rent burden and housing type determine benefit eligibility. The benefit freezes eligible rent increases; it does not allocate an apartment.
The benefit covers eligible increases while the household remains qualified. The apartment’s lease and underlying rent-regulation rules continue to apply.

An eligible household member can apply to take over the benefit after the recipient dies or permanently leaves. Benefit takeover has its own qualification and documentation requirements, separate from succession to the tenancy.

Recipients moving to another rent-regulated apartment can apply after moving to transfer their benefit. Qualification and the new apartment’s legal rent govern the transfer and possible frozen-rent adjustment. This transfers a benefit, not an apartment assignment.

programs.label: CityFHEPS
programs.purpose: Helps eligible households pay part of the monthly rent and remain housed.
programs.scope: NYC-administered assistance; supported destinations include places outside NYC within New York State. Caseload is not an NYC market-exposure denominator.
programs.rent_regulation: Separate layer; not inferred from program identity
programs.policy_status: 2026 payment schedule operational rules include package and lease timing; see Payment rules
programs.finding: NYC effect not estimated. Available evidence does not identify rent changes for comparable unassisted units.
programs.statistic_note: Comparable caseload and rent statistics have not been verified for this release.

entries.text: CityFHEPS supports eligible households moving or remaining in place. HRA reports assistance for up to five years; continuing assistance depends on program renewal rules.

The NYC schedule is a ceiling when all utilities are included, not actual rent, tenant contribution or subsidy expenditure. Utility allowances have separate schedules. Statewide destinations use separate amounts.

Packages submitted through February 28, 2026 may use the 2025 schedule unless the lease begins April 1, 2026 or later. Packages submitted from March 1, 2026, or with an April 1, 2026 lease start, must use the 2026 schedule. Consult DSS for later lease dates and renewal-specific application.

DSS checks legal regulated rents and compares market rents with similar units. Required applications must pass review; renewals may also require review. An excessive proposal can be reduced. Side payments above the approved contract rent are prohibited.

assessment.outcome: Rent change for comparable unassisted units
assessment.finding: NYC effect not estimated. Program caseloads and market listings do not identify rent changes for comparable unassisted units.
details: Observed: CityFHEPS caseloads, federal county snapshots and monthly StreetEasy market trends are descriptive. CityFHEPS destination geography is unresolved, so no borough exposure or correlation with borough rents is calculated.

Published research: Eriksen and Ross (2015) found no overall rental-price effect of voucher expansion, with the largest increases near voucher ceilings in supply-inelastic cities. Their result is not a CityFHEPS coefficient and may reflect recipient sorting into more expensive units.

Conditional scenarios require take-up, incremental housing demand, rental stock, supply response and a time horizon. No-effect is possible if assistance adds no net demand. Numerical NYC scenario ranges are withheld because these parameters are not established. Scenario sensitivity is not a statistical confidence interval.

Causal assessment: an event study would need actual application, lease and operational dates, pre-policy exposure and credible comparison areas or rent segments. Check pre-trends, concurrent policies, boundary changes and spillovers into controls. Payment standards respond to earlier rents; they are not automatically external shocks. Include decreases as well as increases.

Bunching at a ceiling is a mechanism diagnostic, not proof of harm to unassisted renters. Housing quality, recipient sorting and landlord participation are rival explanations. Rent freezes, host payments and project-based construction need separate mechanisms.
A credible, precise comparison excluding a meaningful rent increase would weaken the positive-spillover hypothesis. Wide intervals indicate uncertainty, not proof of no effect.

availability.detail: DSS/HRA target: actual paid amounts and adjustments, separate from budget allocations and payment ceilings. Public schedule is not expenditure.

availability.field: Approved rent and applicable payment standard
availability.detail: DSS/HRA target: approved contract amount and schedule used, with application and lease dates. Published ceiling schedule is verified separately.
DSS-34 confirms the review process and comparison tool. Access to case results and comparable-unit records is unconfirmed; investigate an authorized agency extract.
Agency-held linkage key requested only where releasable. No household identity guesses or joins to anonymous survey respondents.
Request agency-coded status and borough or suppressed tract/month aggregates. HCR unit records remain an access dependency.

availability.field: Comparable rental panel with assistance status
availability.detail: No verified public panel here identifies assistance status, repeated unit rents, characteristics and dates. Public listings are not proof of unassisted tenancy.
DSS-8r: 2025/2026 NYC ceilings and utility allowances with package and lease timing rules; not actual payments.
HUD Picture 2025 county extract and dictionary. Program/subprogram and missing codes preserved; snapshot cannot by itself support an event study.

availability.field: Monthly market asking rents and inventory
availability.detail: StreetEasy borough/city series ingested; assistance status unknown. Existing Zillow ZIP ZORI is a different repeat-rent index and is not averaged into borough medians.
ACS B25003 renter-occupied housing and NYCHVS occupied-renter estimates are candidate denominators. A matched-vintage monthly borough denominator is not established; do not divide unaligned series.
DCP Housing Database is the candidate completion source; match completion dates and borough/tract boundaries before fitting. No matched control panel is assembled here.

scenarios.name: Incremental demand with supply response
scenarios.sensitivity: For fixed stock and demand elasticity, lower take-up or incremental demand reduces the conditional effect; higher supply elasticity reduces it. Use conditional_scenario with disclosed parameters.
